issues.legal_issue: A claim based on a later adoption is not strictly barred as res judicata by an earlier consent decree, although it asserts the same right as the earlier claim.
material_facts: An earlier dispute over the claimant’s status as an adopted son was resolved by a decree made in terms of a compromise.
The later claim relied on an adoption that occurred after the earlier compromise decree.
The claimant asserted the same right to the family property as an adopted son, but on the basis of the later adoption.
issues.conclusion: The consent decree did not strictly bar the later suit as res judicata under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, although the later claim was made in the same right as the earlier one. The decree’s effect as an estoppel was considered separately.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply in terms to a consent decree because the issues have not been heard and finally decided in the statutory sense. A later suit asserting the same right may be barred despite reliance on a different ground; the court relied on Mt. Sardaran v. Shiv Lal, AIR 1944 Lah 282 (FB), and distinguished the reasoning in Mahadevappa v. Dharmappa, AIR 1942 Bom 322, which turned on the later claim not having been available in the earlier suit. A consent decree may nevertheless raise an estoppel, as discussed in the commentary on section 11.

predicates.adoption_property_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking family property on the basis of an asserted adoption.
predicates.earlier_decree_was_compromise_decree: The earlier dispute was resolved by a decree made in terms of a compromise.
predicates.later_claim_based_on_later_adoption: The claimant based the later claim on an adoption occurring after the earlier dispute was resolved.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks family property based on a later adoption after an earlier compromise decree, the later claim is not strictly barred as res judicata.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who accepted a benefit in reliance on a representation in a compromise decree that an adoption right was lost cannot later assert that right to obtain relief.
material_facts: The compromise decree stated that the widow’s right to adopt had been lost from the beginning and that the claimant could not obtain the family property.
The defendant paid the claimant a lump sum in consideration of the compromise and relied on the representation about the adoption right.
The claimant accepted the payment and relinquished claims to the family property.
The claimant later relied on a new adoption to claim the family property.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was estopped from asserting that the widow had a right to adopt him, and the suit was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Evidence Act bars a person from denying a representation of fact that the person caused or permitted another to believe and act upon to their detriment. The court construed the compromise decree’s declaration that the adoption right was lost from the beginning as a representation of fact, not merely an expression of future intention. Estoppel could apply even if the arrangement also amounted to an agreement, to prevent fraud or circuity of action; the court relied on Bigelow on Estoppel, 6th Edition, pages 639–640.
